title: Bonhoeffer's prison questions
hook: in prison he asked who Christ is for us today

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barth's simple summary: a whole theology, the story says, in a children's song. Your line was Jesus loves me. What did you manage to say in one sentence? Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

A prison cell in Berlin. Letters go out with the help of guards willing to carry them. The prisoner is Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran pastor, held by the Nazi regime and connected to the resistance against it. Outside, the war goes on. Inside, he writes to his friend Eberhard Bethge, and in one of those letters he puts down a question he can't stop turning over: who is Christ really, for us today? Not a question for a seminar. A question asked by a man who didn't know if he'd see the outside again. Today, Bonhoeffer's prison questions.

Bonhoeffer wasn't asking what Christ meant for people long ago, or what the creeds say in the abstract. He was asking what Christ means for a world where people no longer felt they needed religion to explain things. In his letters he tried out bold phrases, like religionless Christianity, and he warned against using God as a stopgap: a God who only shows up at the edges, where our knowledge runs out or our strength gives way. God, he wrote, should be found at the center of life, not only at its edges: in strength as well as weakness, in health and not only in a crisis. In notes for a book he never finished, he called Jesus the man for others, and said the church is only the church when it exists for others. He didn't live to work it out. He was executed by the Nazi regime before the war ended, and the questions stayed open. Christians still read them differently. Some hear a call to a quieter, more worldly faith, lived out in plain service. Others point out that in another letter he named prayer and doing what is right as the heart of being a Christian in his time, and hear a call to costly discipleship. The question itself is old. Jesus asked his own disciples near Caesarea Philippi: "But whom say ye that I am?" Bonhoeffer heard it again, in a cell, with the world on fire around him.
screen: `WHO IS CHRIST FOR US TODAY?` · `AT THE CENTER, NOT THE EDGES` · `THE MAN FOR OTHERS` · `BUT WHOM SAY YE THAT I AM?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask it yourself. Settle, and breathe. Let Bonhoeffer's question sit in the room with you: who is Christ, for us today? Then bring it smaller and closer. Not for the whole world. For this week, in the life you actually have. If you follow Jesus, notice what answer comes, and what answer you wish would come. If you don't, ask what his life seems to mean to the people you know who do, or what it might ask of anyone. There's no need to land anywhere. Just keep the question company. The bell holds the time.
Bonhoeffer's prison questions. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's letters from a Nazi prison, asking who Christ really is for people today.
Your line: who is Christ today? Today, write the question somewhere you'll see it, and before bed jot down one honest answer, even a short one. Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Bonhoeffer's prison letters, published after his death, are read in study groups, sermons and retreats; some Christians keep his question in front of them as a way of examining how their faith meets daily life.

notes: All Bonhoeffer material is paraphrased (Letters and Papers from Prison is under copyright in English translation). 'Who is Christ really, for us today?' is given without quotation marks as a paraphrase of the letter to Bethge; confirm.
'God as a stopgap' and 'at the center of life, not only at its edges' paraphrase the prison letters; confirm fair.
'The man for others' and 'the church is only the church when it exists for others' paraphrase the 'Outline for a Book'; confirm.
'Prayer and doing what is right' paraphrases the baptism letter for his godson; confirm.
